story.started: More than 20 years of personal publishing
story.idea:
Jamie started blogging when writing on the web was becoming a common way to share ideas. He discovered that he enjoyed writing in public: telling stories about his experiences and sharing the projects he was working on. That enjoyment became a habit that continues today.

With roughly 10,000 posts across more than 20 years, the blog is a long-running record of one person’s life. It is personal and noncommercial, bringing together everyday experiences, photographs, and things Jamie builds.

The blog has moved from .Text, a Windows .NET blogging package, through WordPress to Micro.blog. Its writing has expanded from mainly longer articles to include shorter updates and, increasingly, photographs as mobile publishing made sharing them easier. It is a foundation for the wider collection, and its posts are syndicated in Weekly Thing.

things.title: R/W Book Club
things.summary: A shared archive of the Read / Write Book Club’s reading.

story.introduction: A long-running reading group, with a shared record.
engineering: The website presents the club’s reading history and members’ commentary.
Public llms.txt and llms-full.txt files make the reading record accessible to agents for analysis.
An iCal feed lets members subscribe to the meeting calendar.
Earlier approaches included MediaWiki and a shared Airtable database.
questions: How can an agent explore the club’s reading history?
How has the book club website evolved?
story.idea:
R/W stands for Read / Write Book Club. The club was started by Jamie’s professor, Dr. John Riedl; Jamie joined when the group was replacing a member. Jamie built the website, not the club.

The members have been meeting for many years, reading mostly nonfiction across a variety of subjects. The website documents the books they have read and provides a shared place for members’ commentary.

The group’s reading record has taken several forms, including a MediaWiki site and an Airtable database used across the club. The current website makes that history accessible to both people and agents: LLM context files provide an easily parsed reading record, and an iCal feed puts meetings on members’ calendars. The website shares an interest in reading with Jamie’s Reading Things newsletter.

things.title: Road Sign Math
things.summary: Find an equation hiding in plain sight.

story.introduction: A little mathematics. A lot of looking around.
engineering: Historical wiki content is recovered into structured Markdown, with numbers, equations, places, and photo provenance.
The recovered collection includes 251 signs, alongside the original rules and other project pages.
Recovered images distinguish camera originals, archived originals, poster crops, and missing photos.
questions: How was Road Sign Math recovered?
story.idea: A driving game with a simple invitation: find a road sign whose numbers make a valid equation, photograph it, and share the discovery. The historical project now has a locally recovered archive of signs and images.
